analysis.investment_thesis: ACME Solar's renewable energy story sounds compelling — India's solar capacity needs to multiply many times over — but the financial reality is ugly: revenue has declined at -4.6% CAGR for 5 years, ROCE is only 8.42% (barely covering cost of capital), D/E is 2.72 with INR 12,998 Cr of borrowings consuming INR 759 Cr in annual interest, and free cash flow was -INR 1,719 Cr in FY25 as capex devours cash. I'm not buying a capital-destruction machine at 37x earnings.
key_strengths: Operating margin of 65.28% is characteristic of long-term PPAs with government-backed off-takers — predictable cash at the operating level
5/5 years of positive operating cash flow (INR 1,543 Cr in FY25) shows the existing assets do generate cash
Pipeline of 3,780 MW under development could double operating capacity and eventually drive revenue growth
key_risks: Revenue declining at -4.6% CAGR over 5 years — the growth story exists only in future capacity, not current results
Debt load of INR 12,998 Cr (borrowings) with finance cost of INR 759 Cr vs operating income of INR 1,237 Cr leaves razor-thin interest coverage
FY24 net profit of INR 698 Cr was distorted by INR 891 Cr 'Other Income' (likely asset monetization) — normalized earnings are far lower, making P/E 37x even more expensive
red_flags: Free cash flow -INR 1,719 Cr in FY25 — the company is burning through the IPO proceeds at an alarming pace
ROE of only 7.57% despite 2.72x leverage — leverage should amplify returns, but here it's destroying them
Revenue has contracted every year from 2020 to 2025; the growth thesis is entirely dependent on future commissioning
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Every investor loves the renewable energy story, and India's solar ambition is real — but loving a sector and loving a stock are different things. ACME Solar's revenues have fallen from INR 1,777 Cr (FY20) to INR 1,405 Cr (FY25), EBITDA dropped nearly 10% CAGR over the same period, and the company relies on massive debt (D/E 2.72) and new equity raises to fund its pipeline. The IPO proceeds are visible in the equity jump (INR 2,591 Cr → INR 4,784 Cr) and cash balance (INR 309 Cr → INR 1,252 Cr), but borrowings also jumped from INR 8,536 Cr to INR 12,998 Cr simultaneously.

At P/E 37x on unreliable earnings (one-off items drove FY24 profits) and P/S of 9.4x on declining revenue, I'm being asked to pay a premium for a business that hasn't yet proven it can grow. Utility-scale solar is a commodity business — no pricing power, massive capital intensity, government-dependent revenues. I'll pass and watch from the sidelines until the new capacity translates into growing, consistent earnings.
